topic: Why Belgium Is Stranger Than You Think (Vennbahn)
hook: Your bike path in Belgium runs through Germany, and every metre of it still belongs to Belgium.
title: Why Belgium Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
A Belgian bike path cuts through Germany, and that is only the start. Six true facts about Belgium: three languages, 541 days without a government, the longest tram line in the world, Antwerp's diamonds, a land that belonged to nobody, and the Vennbahn railway strip inside Germany.

#Belgium #Geography #FactsThatSoundFake
comment_prompt: Which fact surprised you most: one to six?

chapters.title: The longest tram line on Earth
Antwerp and the Indian diamond link
The land that belonged to nobody

scenes.narration: Your bike path in Belgium runs through Germany, and every metre of it still belongs to Belgium.
scenes.headline: Belgium Inside Germany
scenes.sub: A bike path with a secret

scenes.narration: Step off that path and you are in German villages. Stay on it and you never leave Belgium.
scenes.headline: Two Countries, One Path

scenes.narration: And this is just one oddity in a country that is smaller than the Indian state of Kerala.
scenes.headline: Smaller Than Kerala

scenes.narration: Today I will show you six facts about Belgium that sound fake but are completely true.
scenes.headline: 6 True Facts

scenes.narration: And by the end, you will see exactly how a Belgian railway ended up cutting through Germany.
scenes.headline: The Big One Is Last

scenes.narration: Let us start with a country that cannot even agree on how to say hello.
scenes.headline: Let's Begin

scenes.narration: Chapter one. Belgium has three official languages, and one small country has to juggle all of them.
scenes.headline: Three Languages

scenes.narration: In the north, people speak Dutch. In the south, people speak French. In a small eastern corner, people speak German.
scenes.headline: Dutch, French, German

scenes.narration: Yes, German. A small part of eastern Belgium speaks German every day and even has its own government.
scenes.headline: German Inside Belgium

scenes.narration: Belgium covers about thirty thousand square kilometres. Kerala is bigger than that, yet Belgium fits three languages.
scenes.headline: Smaller Than Kerala

scenes.narration: Even the capital, Brussels, uses two languages on its signs, so one road can have two different names.
scenes.headline: One Road, Two Names

scenes.narration: Think of a city sign in two languages, but with each language belonging to a different part of the country.
scenes.headline: Signs In Two Languages

scenes.narration: There is even a language border across the country, fixed by law in the early nineteen sixties.
scenes.headline: A Language Border

scenes.narration: Cross that line, and the official language of schools and government offices changes.
scenes.headline: Cross It, Language Changes

scenes.narration: Belgium even has six governments for under twelve million people. That is a lot of ministers.
scenes.headline: Six Governments

scenes.narration: And all those governments lead us to chapter two, which is even stranger.
scenes.headline: It Gets Stranger

scenes.narration: Chapter two. Imagine a country running for almost a year and a half without a real government.
scenes.headline: No Government

scenes.narration: Belgium did exactly that. After elections in June 2010, the parties could not agree on a new government.
scenes.headline: Election, June 2010

scenes.narration: It took five hundred and forty one days before a new government was sworn in, in December 2011.
scenes.headline: 541 Days

scenes.narration: That is more than a year and four months. A full election, and nobody could form a team.
scenes.headline: Over 1.5 Years

scenes.narration: The north and the south wanted very different things, and the talks kept breaking down.
scenes.headline: Talks Kept Failing

scenes.narration: Yet trains ran, schools opened, and salaries were paid, because a caretaker government kept daily work going.
scenes.headline: Life Went On

scenes.narration: Some people joked that Belgium works fine without a government. Of course, that is only a joke.
scenes.headline: Just A Joke

scenes.narration: People held protests and demanded their leaders end the deadlock, and the long wait became world news.
scenes.headline: World News

scenes.narration: For Indian viewers, imagine no new Prime Minister for one and a half years after a general election.
scenes.headline: Imagine This In India

scenes.narration: It is hard to picture, but it really happened in a rich European country.
scenes.headline: It Really Happened

scenes.narration: Now let us leave politics and go to the coast, where a vehicle breaks a world record.
scenes.headline: To The Coast

scenes.narration: Stay with me, because the biggest surprise is still waiting at the end.
scenes.headline: Stay Till The End

scenes.narration: Chapter three. Belgium has a tram that runs along its whole coastline, and it is the longest tram line in the world.
scenes.headline: Longest Tram Line

scenes.narration: It is called the Kusttram, which simply means the coast tram.
scenes.headline: The Kusttram

scenes.narration: It runs from De Panne near the French border all the way to Knokke-Heist near the Dutch border.
scenes.headline: De Panne To Knokke

scenes.narration: That is about sixty-eight kilometres, which is more like a train journey than a city tram ride.
scenes.headline: About 68 Kilometres

scenes.narration: A tram is usually a short city ride, but this one runs beside the sea for hours.
scenes.headline: A Tram By The Sea

scenes.narration: You sit by the window with the North Sea on one side and beach towns on the other.
scenes.headline: Sea Views All Way

scenes.narration: It stops at many small beach towns, so you can hop off for an ice cream and hop back on.
scenes.headline: Hop On, Hop Off

scenes.narration: Most countries use trams inside one city. Belgium stretched one along its entire coast.
scenes.headline: A Whole Coast

scenes.narration: A tram that lasts for hours is odd, but the next chapter is about something that glitters.
scenes.headline: Now Something Shiny

scenes.narration: Chapter four has an Indian connection that most people never hear about.
scenes.headline: An Indian Connection

scenes.narration: One Belgian city handles most of the world's rough diamonds, and it is not anywhere near a diamond mine.
scenes.headline: Diamond Capital

scenes.narration: It is Antwerp. Rough stones arrive from mines, and traders there buy, sell, and send them out again.
scenes.headline: Antwerp

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places and facts like these, this is a good moment to subscribe, because there is more coming.
scenes.headline: Subscribe For More

scenes.narration: Now here is the part Indian viewers will love. Many diamond traders in Antwerp come from Gujarati families.
scenes.headline: Gujarat In Antwerp

scenes.narration: Families from places like Palanpur moved to Antwerp decades ago, and Indian businesses became a major force there.
scenes.headline: Indian Traders

scenes.narration: Surat, back in India, is where a huge share of the world's diamonds are cut and polished.
scenes.headline: Surat Cuts The Stones

scenes.narration: So a stone can be traded in Belgium, polished in Gujarat, and worn at a wedding anywhere in the world.
scenes.headline: From Mine To Wedding

scenes.narration: A walk through the Antwerp diamond district shows shops and offices packed into just a few streets.
scenes.headline: A Few Busy Streets

scenes.narration: Big deals there have long been sealed with a handshake and a word of good luck.
scenes.headline: A Handshake Deal

scenes.narration: Next is a place that was once a territory no single country owned, and it nearly spoke Esperanto.
scenes.headline: Nobody's Land

scenes.narration: Chapter five. For about a hundred years, a tiny patch of land near Belgium belonged to no single country.
scenes.headline: Land Of Nobody

scenes.narration: It was called Neutral Moresnet, and it was one of the smallest territories in Europe.
scenes.headline: Neutral Moresnet

scenes.narration: After Napoleon was defeated, Prussia and the Netherlands could not agree who should get this small zinc mine area.
scenes.headline: Nobody Could Decide

scenes.narration: So they did the simple thing. They agreed to share it, and it stayed that way for about a hundred years.
scenes.headline: They Shared It

scenes.narration: Later, Belgium took the Dutch side after it became independent, so Belgium and Prussia shared it together.
scenes.headline: Belgium Joins In

scenes.narration: The zinc mine made the land valuable, and workers and their families lived there under shared rule.
scenes.headline: A Zinc Mine Town

scenes.narration: It was so small that you could walk across it in a short time.
scenes.headline: Tiny Enough To Walk

scenes.narration: Around 1908, a local doctor named Wilhelm Molly pushed a bold idea. He wanted it to become an Esperanto country.
scenes.headline: Doctor Molly's Plan

scenes.narration: Esperanto is a language invented so that people from every country could talk to each other.
scenes.headline: A Language For All

scenes.narration: They even planned to rename the place Amikejo, which means place of friendship.
scenes.headline: Amikejo

scenes.narration: The plan never fully worked. After the First World War, the Treaty of Versailles gave Moresnet to Belgium.
scenes.headline: Versailles Ends It

scenes.narration: That same treaty is the key to our last chapter, so remember it.
scenes.headline: Remember This Treaty

scenes.narration: Because it also decided who got a railway, and that is where Belgium gets truly strange.
scenes.headline: A Railway Is Next

scenes.narration: Chapter six, the biggest one. A railway that Belgium owns, running through German land.
scenes.headline: The Vennbahn

scenes.narration: It is called the Vennbahn, and Germany built it long ago to carry coal and iron.
scenes.headline: Built By Germany

scenes.narration: After the First World War, the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 gave the railway line to Belgium.
scenes.headline: Given To Belgium

scenes.narration: But the line did not stay inside Belgium. It kept crossing the border, in and out of Germany.
scenes.headline: In And Out Of Germany

scenes.narration: So Belgium did not just get a railway. It got the land under the tracks, even where that land was German.
scenes.headline: The Land Under The Tracks

scenes.narration: Picture a thin strip of Belgium running through German countryside, like a ribbon laid across the map.
scenes.headline: A Ribbon Of Belgium

scenes.narration: German villages sit on both sides of that strip, with German homes close to a Belgian track.
scenes.headline: German Villages Both Sides

scenes.narration: Trains stopped running long ago, and the old railway became a cycle path about a hundred and twenty five kilometres long.
scenes.headline: Now A Cycle Path

scenes.narration: It is a popular cycle route, running through forests, hills and small towns.
scenes.headline: Forests And Hills

scenes.narration: And yes, if you cycle it, you pass through Germany while staying on a path that belongs to Belgium.
scenes.headline: Germany, But Belgian

scenes.narration: There are no passport checks on the way, since Belgium, Germany and Luxembourg are all in the Schengen area.
scenes.headline: No Passport Checks

scenes.narration: The path even reaches Luxembourg, so one ride can touch three countries.
scenes.headline: Three Countries

scenes.narration: The route starts in Aachen, in Germany, and ends in Troisvierges, in Luxembourg.
scenes.headline: Aachen To Troisvierges

scenes.narration: The strip is Belgian, but the homes, shops and farms on either side are German.
scenes.headline: Belgian Strip, German Homes

scenes.narration: So the opening line is true. Yes, you can cycle through Germany and never leave Belgium.
scenes.headline: It Is True

scenes.narration: That was Belgium: three languages, and a government that took five hundred and forty one days to form.
scenes.headline: Belgium Recap

scenes.narration: A record-breaking coast tram, a diamond city with Indian roots, and a land that belonged to nobody.
scenes.headline: Tram, Diamonds, Nobody's Land

scenes.narration: And a railway strip Belgium owns, cutting through Germany. Your bike path in Belgium really does run through Germany.
scenes.headline: Belgium Inside Germany

scenes.narration: Tomorrow: a country that sits on two continents at once.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow
